meta.description: Not Byron. The earliest strong match is Thomas Hood in The Athenaeum, 22 April 1837 — Byron's real Beppo line says something else entirely.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Easy Reading Is Hard Writing'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Byron. Earliest strong match: Thomas Hood, The Athenaeum, 22 April 1837. Byron's Beppo line is different — and is why the credit drifted.

answer.label: Not Lord Byron — earliest strong match is Thomas Hood
answer.sourceLine: Byron never wrote this. The earliest strong match documented by Quote Investigator is Thomas Hood, who put “the easiest reading is d__d hard writing” — already inside quotation marks, as something in circulation — in his letter “Copyright and Copywrong,” printed in The Athenaeum on 22 April 1837. Byron’s real line, in Beppo (1818), is the wish “Oh that I had the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading!” — which is very probably where the misattribution began.

source.heading: The earliest documented appearance

docMeta.dd: Thomas Hood, letter to the editor of The Athenaeum, 22 April 1837
“Oh that I had the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading!” — Beppo, A Venetian Story (1818)
Proverbial — Hood set it in quotation marks, so it was already circulating

source.excerpt: And firstly, as to how he writes, upon which head there is a wonderful diversity of opinions; one thinks that writing is “as easy as lying,” and pictures the author sitting carefully at his desk “with his glove on,” like Sir Roger de Coverley’s poetical ancestor. A second holds that “the easiest reading is d__d hard writing,” and imagines Time himself beating his brains over an extempore.
trail: 1772 — the opposite maxim. Richard Brinsley Sheridan’s “Clio’s Protest,” circulated by 1772, carries the couplet “You write with ease, to shew your breeding; / But easy writing’s vile hard reading.” The words are the same; the argument is reversed. Quote Investigator ↗

1818 — Byron, and the seed of the error. In Beppo Byron writes “Oh that I had the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading!” — a wish, not a maxim, and with no ‘hard writing’ anywhere near it. Read the passage at Wikisource ↗
22 April 1837 — the first print sighting. Thomas Hood, in The Athenaeum: “the easiest reading is d__d hard writing,” quoted as something people say. The Athenaeum, p. 287 ↗

1884 onward — the famous names. A Daily News reviewer gives it to Byron in 1884; The Engineering Magazine gives it to Thackeray in 1898; Maya Angelou gives it to Hawthorne in 1979 and again in 1990. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗
source.excerptNote: The Athenaeum censored “damned” to “d__d.” Note Hood’s own quotation marks: he is reporting a saying, not minting one. The tidy modern wording — “easy reading is hard writing” — appears unattributed eight years later, in an 1845 book review in Douglas Jerrold’s Shilling Magazine.

source.rightsNote: The wording is a proverb rather than one author’s property, and every documented source for it is long out of copyright in the United States: Hood’s letter in The Athenaeum (1837), the unattributed “easy reading is hard writing” in Douglas Jerrold’s Shilling Magazine (1845), and Charles Allston Collins’s use of it in All the Year Round (1860) all predate 1931 by a wide margin. Byron’s Beppo (1818) is likewise public domain.

author.name: Thomas Hood
author.kicker: The man who wrote it down first
author.heading: Who was Thomas Hood?
author.bio: Thomas Hood was an English poet, editor and humorist, born in London on 23 May 1799 and dead there on 3 May 1845, best remembered now for The Song of the Shirt and The Bridge of Sighs. He was a regular contributor to The Athenaeum, and his 1837 letters to its editor under the title “Copyright and Copywrong” argued the writer’s case in the copyright fight of the day. He is the first person known to have set this maxim in print — though he framed it as a saying he was repeating, not one he had coined.

misattribution.heading: Everyone who has been handed this line
misattribution.intro: Few maxims have been passed around as promiscuously as this one. Because it flatters writers, it gets pinned on whichever famous writer the speaker admires — and because a near-identical saying runs in the opposite direction, even the careful get it backwards.

items.why: Byron wrote “Oh that I had the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading!” in Beppo (1818). He used the words ‘easy writing’ and ‘easy reading’ and neither ‘hard writing’ nor ‘hard reading’ — he was wishing for a gift, not describing a cost. Quote Investigator judges those lines the probable source of the confusion, and records a London Daily News review of 21 August 1884 asserting “as Byron used to say, easy reading means hard writing.” Quote Investigator ↗

items.scope: The modern credit, via Maya Angelou
items.why: Angelou quoted “Easy reading is damned hard writing” at a Richmond press conference in 1979 and again in her 1990 Paris Review interview, crediting Hawthorne both times. Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence for Hawthorne, and Wikiquote lists it under his Disputed heading ↗, noting the line is also attributed to Ernest Hemingway.

Sheridan really did write, in “Clio’s Protest” (circulated by 1772), “You write with ease, to shew your breeding; / But easy writing’s vile hard reading.” That is the opposite claim — easy writing makes hard reading. Graham’s American Monthly Magazine in 1849 and the Methodist Quarterly Review in 1867 both handed him the inverted version instead. Quote Investigator ↗
A book review in the New York Engineering Magazine in 1898 opened “‘Easy reading means hard writing,’ said Thackeray” — an attribution nothing in the earlier record supports. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that it is a proverb with a first witness rather than an author: Thomas Hood printed it in The Athenaeum on 22 April 1837 and put quotation marks round it, meaning he was already repeating it. Quote Investigator provisionally credits Hood ↗ while noting an earlier source may yet surface.

context.heading: Why this one keeps changing hands
lead: There are really two mirrored sayings here, and almost every misattribution comes from confusing them. The older one is a put-down: writing that came easily is painful to read. The newer one is a compliment turned inside out: prose that reads easily cost somebody enormous effort. Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote the first; Thomas Hood is the earliest person known to have printed the second.

Byron sits between them, which is exactly why his name attached itself. In Beppo he wished aloud for “the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading” — both halves of the vocabulary, none of the argument. Quote Investigator judges those lines the probable source of the confusion, and by 1884 a London reviewer was simply asserting that “as Byron used to say, easy reading means hard writing.”
detailsBody: After Hood, the saying travelled without an owner. An 1845 book review in Douglas Jerrold’s Shilling Magazine used the now-familiar wording — “easy reading is hard writing” — with no attribution at all, and Thomas Keightley’s 1848 Horace has “easy reading is usually very hard writing.” In 1851 a Washington reviewer credited it to “the schoolboy.”

Then the famous names arrived. Graham’s American Monthly Magazine pinned a garbled version on Sheridan in 1849 and the Methodist Quarterly Review did the same in 1867. Charles Allston Collins called it a “rule” in Dickens’s All the Year Round in 1860; Anthony Trollope gave a character the thought “Easy reading requires hard writing” in Kept in the Dark (1882). Byron got the credit in 1884, Thackeray in 1898.

The modern chain runs through Maya Angelou, who quoted it at a Richmond press conference in 1979 and again in her 1990 Paris Review interview, crediting Nathaniel Hawthorne both times. Nothing in the record supports Hawthorne, and Wikiquote files the line under Hawthorne’s “Disputed” heading, noting it is also thrown at Ernest Hemingway.
context.pull: Byron wished for the art of easy writing. He never said that easy reading was hard writing.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's chronology credits Thomas Hood's 22 April 1837 Athenaeum letter 'Copyright and Copywrong' as the earliest strong match ('the easiest reading is d__d hard writing'), lists the 1845 Douglas Jerrold's Shilling Magazine, 1848 Keightley, 1849 Graham's (to Sheridan), 1851 Daily National Intelligencer, 1860 All the Year Round, 1867 Methodist Quarterly Review (to Sheridan), 1882 Trollope, 1884 Daily News (to Byron), 1898 Engineering Magazine (to Thackeray), and 1979/1990 Maya Angelou (to Hawthorne) instances, and states there is no substantive evidence Byron or Sheridan used this maxim.

Quote Investigator documents Sheridan's 'Clio's Protest' couplet ('You write with ease, to shew your breeding; / But easy writing's vile hard reading', circulated by 1772) and Byron's 1818 Beppo lines 'Oh that I had the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading!'
The full text of Byron's Beppo contains the lines 'Oh that I had the art of easy writing / What should be easy reading!' (stanza LI in this edition).
Page 287 of the 1837 volume of The Athenaeum contains the phrase 'hard writing,' followed by 'and imagines Time him-self...' — matching Hood's 'Copyright and Copywrong' letter.

Wikiquote lists 'Easy reading is damn hard writing.' in Nathaniel Hawthorne's Disputed section, noting it is also attributed to Ernest Hemingway and others, and that Wikiquote's own earliest definite occurrence is Maya Angelou in Conversations With Maya Angelou (1989).
Thomas Hood was an English poet, author and humorist, born 23 May 1799 in London and died 3 May 1845 in London, and was a regular contributor to the Athenaeum.
Wikiquote's Lord Byron page contains an entry for 'easy reading is hard writing' (checked as a possible sourced or misattributed listing).
The Paris Review's Maya Angelou interview (Art of Fiction No. 119) contains her attribution of 'Easy reading is damn hard writing' to Nathaniel Hawthorne.
